subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on Food Choice, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain Food Choice for GCSE Edexcel Food Preparation & Nutrition simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an economic factor affecting food choice?
options: Having a limited weekly food budget
questions.explain: Cost and income are economic factors: a limited budget affects what foods a person can afford. Taste, religion and allergies are other, separate factors.

questions.q: A busy worker often buys ready meals rather than cooking from scratch. Which factor most explains this?
questions.explain: Lifestyle factors such as a busy schedule and limited time influence choice, leading people to pick convenience foods that are quick to prepare.

questions.q: What does PAL stand for?
questions.explain: PAL (Physical Activity Level) describes how active a person is. A higher PAL means more energy is used, so more food energy is needed.

questions.q: How does a high physical activity level affect a person's food needs?
options: They need less energy from food
It has no effect on food needs
They need more energy from food
questions.explain: A more active person (higher PAL), such as an athlete, uses more energy, so they need a greater energy intake, often from more carbohydrate and protein.

questions.q: Meat prepared according to Islamic law is described as:
questions.explain: Halal means 'permitted' in Islam; halal meat is slaughtered according to Islamic law. Pork and alcohol are haram (forbidden).

questions.q: In Judaism, which combination of foods is NOT allowed under kosher rules?
options: Meat and dairy in the same meal
questions.explain: Kosher rules forbid mixing meat and dairy, and prohibit pork and shellfish. Meat must be slaughtered and prepared according to Jewish law.

questions.q: A person who eats no meat or fish but does eat eggs and dairy is a:
questions.explain: A lacto-ovo vegetarian avoids meat and fish but eats dairy (lacto) and eggs (ovo). A vegan avoids all animal products.

questions.q: Which label shows a product supports better prices and conditions for producers in developing countries?
questions.explain: The Fairtrade mark shows farmers and workers in developing countries received fairer prices and conditions. Choosing it is an ethical food choice.

questions.q: A person with coeliac disease must avoid which substance?
questions.explain: People with coeliac disease have an immune reaction to gluten (in wheat, barley and rye), so they must follow a gluten-free diet.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a food allergy and a food intolerance?
options: An allergy involves the immune system and can be life-threatening
An intolerance is always more dangerous
questions.explain: A food allergy is an immune-system reaction that can be severe (anaphylaxis), e.g. to nuts. An intolerance (e.g. lactose) causes discomfort but does not involve the immune system in the same way.

questions.q: Which piece of information is legally required on a pre-packed food label?
questions.explain: By law, pre-packed food labels must show the name, ingredients list, allergen information, weight, storage and a date mark, among other details.

questions.q: On an ingredients list, how must the 14 major allergens be shown?
questions.explain: Law requires the 14 main allergens (e.g. nuts, milk, eggs, gluten) to be emphasised in the ingredients list, usually in bold, so consumers can spot them easily.

questions.q: On a traffic-light nutrition label, what does a red section indicate?
options: The food is high in that nutrient (e.g. fat, sugar or salt)
The food is out of date
The food is low in that nutrient
questions.explain: Red means the food is high in that nutrient (such as fat, saturated fat, sugar or salt); green is low and amber is medium. It helps consumers make healthier choices at a glance.

questions.q: Nutrition information on packaging is usually given per 100g so that shoppers can:
questions.explain: Giving values per 100g lets shoppers compare the nutritional content of different products fairly, regardless of pack size.

questions.q: Which is a marketing technique used to encourage people to buy a food product?
options: Special offers such as 'buy one get one free'
Making the packaging plain and dull
Hiding the product at the back of the shop
questions.explain: Offers like BOGOF, eye-catching packaging, adverts and product placement are marketing techniques designed to influence what shoppers buy.

questions.q: Placing sweets at the checkout is a marketing strategy that mainly encourages:
questions.explain: Checkout displays encourage impulse buying, where shoppers make unplanned purchases while queuing. This is why 'junk-free' checkouts have been introduced in some shops.

questions.q: Sensory evaluation of food uses which of the senses?
options: Sight, smell, taste, touch and hearing
questions.explain: Sensory evaluation uses all five senses: appearance (sight), aroma (smell), flavour (taste), texture (touch/mouthfeel) and sound (e.g. crunch).

questions.q: Why should sensory tests be carried out under controlled conditions (e.g. same portion size, coded samples)?
options: To make results fair, reliable and unbiased
questions.explain: Controlled conditions such as identical portions, random codes and separate booths reduce bias, making the sensory test fair and its results reliable.

questions.q: Which sensory test asks tasters to pick the odd sample out of three?
questions.explain: In a triangle test, tasters are given three samples (two the same, one different) and must identify the odd one out, testing whether they can detect a difference.

questions.q: A company wants tasters to place five yoghurts in order from least to most sweet. Which test should they use?
questions.explain: A ranking test asks tasters to place samples in order for a single characteristic (such as sweetness), which is exactly what is needed here.
